title: Dark square, light square
hook: A checkerboard, a cylinder and its shadow. Which square sends less light?

knows: we see the colours that are there
doesNotKnow: that the brain estimates surface colour by discounting the lighting
so the same light from the screen can look like two different greys

misconception: If two squares look different, they are different on the screen.
objective: The learner can say that squares A and B send the same light (the sampler reads the same value), that the visual system judged B lighter because it discounts the shadow, and that this guess is usually right in a real scene, because light reaching the eye is lighting times reflectance.

claims.text: Squares A and B are painted with exactly the same grey on the screen (brightness 120 of 255).
claims.source: Observation on the screen; the code is the source (strategy section 5, class 3). Demo.tsx draws A, B and the connecting strip from one constant SAME = #787878 (0x78 = 120), not a theme variable, so it is identical in light and dark mode; each cell carries data-fill for checking. The sampler readout prints the value as text. Brief check: company/domains/briefs/checks/big-ideas-cycle1-check.mjs #8.

claims.text: Caption: 'After a well-known checker-shadow illusion. Our own drawing.'
claims.source: Original drawing by the builder (a 5 × 5 checkerboard and a cylinder; not traced). The illusion it follows is Adelson's checker-shadow illusion (Adelson, 1995; described in Adelson, E. H. (2000), 'Lightness perception and lightness illusions', in Gazzaniga (ed.), The New Cognitive Neurosciences, 2nd ed.; to confirm). Per the brief's W-537 re-check, the caption names no one; if Adelson 1995 is confirmed, cm-big-ideas may let it name him. Not opened by the builder.

claims.text: Your visual system knows shadows darken surfaces, so it judged B lighter than the light it sends; that is a guess about the world.
claims.source: Follows from c1 and the learner's own prediction: equal light from A and B was seen as two different greys, so the difference was added by the viewer. The stage stands for the cause: 'Remove the shadow' takes away the cylinder and the shadow while A and B keep their paint. Wording change from the brief: 'lighter than the light it receives' became 'lighter than the light it sends' (the light that comes from B to the eye).

claims.text: Hermann von Helmholtz called perception 'unconscious inference'.
claims.source: Held citation, the lesson's one (class P: public domain). Helmholtz, H. von (1867), Handbuch der physiologischen Optik, vol. 3 ('unbewusster Schluss'; to confirm the section). Not opened by the builder. Cut if not checkable; fallback (brief W-537 re-check): 'Psychologists call this kind of guess an inference.' (no name; support: convention).

claims.text: Where it stops: the light you see is lighting times how much the surface reflects, so a shadowed square sending the same light really is lighter, and in a real scene the guess is usually right.
claims.source: Light reaching the eye = illumination × reflectance. Same light L, shade illumination below sun illumination, so reflectance in shade = L / E_shade > L / E_sun (cycle-1 check script, W-537 block: 0.8 against 0.2 in illustrative units). On the stage the shadow multiplies by 4/7 (210 → 120, 120 → about 69; c6), so B's surface is the light kind. The brief moved the Adelson limit citation off the learner path; the derivation carries the limit.

claims.text: The board's shading (light squares 210 and dark squares 120 in the light; a shadow layer that takes light squares to 120 and dark ones to about 69) is the lesson's model, not a measurement.
claims.source: Demo.tsx constants LIGHT_LIT (210), SAME (120) and SHADOW_OPACITY (3/7: 210 × 4/7 = 120, 120 × 4/7 ≈ 69), a black layer with a blurred edge. Square B is drawn again on top of the shadow from SAME, so its value is exactly 120 by construction. Chosen so that a light square in shadow sends the same value as a dark square in the light.

recall.question: Two sheets of paper send exactly the same light to your camera. One is in shade, one is in sun. Which sheet is whiter?
recall.why: Light reaching the camera is lighting times how much the paper reflects. The shaded sheet gets less light, so to send the same amount it must reflect more: it is the whiter sheet.
